Cutaneous HPV is transcriptionally quiet in skin and carcinoma but productive in warts: a depth-controlled re-mining of public RNA-seq

Author

[Authors to be added]

Published

July 6, 2026

Abstract

Most human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are cutaneous beta- and gamma-types residing on skin as commensals, yet their role in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) remains unsettled, contested between oncogenic “hit-and-run”, protective antiviral immunity, and a virological account in which beta-HPV is transcriptionally restricted by default. Because standard pipelines discard the non-human reads carrying HPV signal, we re-mined public human RNA-seq across skin with a pipeline that screens each library for papillomavirus reads, types positives against the full panel, and scores productive infection from late (L1 major-capsid) transcripts. To control the two confounders, we flagged cell-line and engineered material and scored each library as papillomavirus reads-per-million. HPV signal was concentrated in non-primary material: cell-line and engineered libraries were five-fold enriched for positivity (OR 4.7–5.3, P < 10⁻⁸), dominated by integrated HPV16/HPV18, whereas primary skin carried HPV at only 2–4%. Productive infection was abundant in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (64% of libraries). By contrast, cSCC and actinic keratosis, though sequenced four times more deeply, reached the detection floor in only 1.5% of libraries versus 93.2% of controls (Fisher OR 10,183), with median burden six orders of magnitude lower. Depth-adjusted, neoplasia sat marginally above unselected skin (OR 14, P = 6.7×10⁻⁶), but only as a trace footprint (any-read OR 2.0, P = 5.5×10⁻¹⁰) that deeper sequencing never made productive. A minority of lesions harboured genuine productive gamma-/alpha-HPV infection (HPV12, HPV96, HPV182, HPV16). Cutaneous HPV is productive in warts but quiet in healthy skin and carcinoma: a trace, non-productive footprint that any account of beta-HPV in skin must accommodate. Beyond HPV, this contamination-aware framework, normalised for both sequencing depth and library chemistry, can mine the discarded fraction of public transcriptomes.

Keywords: human papillomavirus; beta-papillomavirus; cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma; skin virome; productive infection; hit-and-run; RNA-seq; public data re-mining; contamination

Introduction

Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are a large and ancient family of small, non-enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses that establish infection in stratified squamous epithelia. More than 220 HPV types have now been fully sequenced and formally classified, partitioned by L1 open-reading-frame identity into five genera: Alpha-, Beta-, Gamma-, Mu- and Nupapillomavirus (Villiers et al. 2004; Bzhalava, Eklund, and Dillner 2015). This genus structure tracks tissue tropism and disease association: the alpha genus contains the mucosal, sexually transmitted types responsible for cervical and other anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers (HPV16, HPV18), whereas the great majority of described types are cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs whose natural habitat is the skin (Villiers et al. 2004; Van Doorslaer et al. 2017). Despite outnumbering the medically prominent alpha types, these cutaneous viruses remain comparatively poorly characterised, and the curated reference genomes that make systematic study possible are consolidated in the Papillomavirus Episteme (PaVE; Van Doorslaer et al. (2017)).

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs behave less like classical pathogens than like members of the commensal skin flora. They are acquired in early life, are ubiquitous on the skin of healthy immunocompetent adults, and persist for months to years as asymptomatic, often low-level infections (Antonsson et al. 2000). Culture-independent surveys of normal-appearing skin reveal striking inter-individual diversity, with multiple co-resident beta- and gamma-genotypes and a continuing discovery of novel types from healthy skin (Foulongne et al. 2012; Nunes, Talpe-Nunes, and Sichero 2018). At DNA level this reservoir is both large and well mapped: shotgun metagenomics of the Human Microbiome Project found HPV in 61.3% of skin samples from healthy subjects, the highest of any body site surveyed (Ma et al. 2014), and type-specific PCR of skin swabs detects beta-HPV in 92% and gamma-HPV in 84% of adults undergoing skin-cancer screening (Rollison, Schell, et al. 2019). Deep sequencing of skin has extended the catalogue to 396 HPV types, 229 of them previously unknown (Bzhalava et al. 2014), so the reservoir is also substantially larger than any reference panel describes. What these DNA-based figures cannot say is whether any of that genetic material is being transcribed. In immunocompetent hosts this carriage is overwhelmingly subclinical: most cutaneous HPV infection lies in a “twilight zone” of latency and immune control rather than producing visible lesions (Doorbar 2023). Yet the composition and frequency of this reservoir in healthy skin remain a basic, incompletely answered descriptive question: which types are actually present, and how often?

A minority of cutaneous infections do become overtly productive and lesional, and two settings define this productive extreme. Common, plantar and flat warts are highly productive infections, driven principally by alpha types HPV2, HPV27 and HPV57, the mu type HPV1, and gamma types such as HPV4, in which abundant virion assembly in the differentiating epidermis produces the koilocytes that are the histological signature of active viral replication (Egawa and Doorbar 2017). Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), or Lewandowsky–Lutz dysplasia, is the second: a rare genodermatosis of selective susceptibility to beta-HPVs that manifests as lifelong flat-wart and pityriasis-versicolor-like lesions, with progression to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) on sun-exposed skin (Orth 2006; Jong, Imahorn, et al. 2018). EV is a Mendelian “experiment of nature”: biallelic loss-of-function in the adjacent keratinocyte genes EVER1/EVER2 (TMC6/TMC8), and subsequently in CIB1, abolishes a keratinocyte-intrinsic restriction of beta-HPV and renders these otherwise-quiescent commensals pathogenic (Ramoz et al. 2002; Lazarczyk et al. 2008; Jong, Créquer, et al. 2018). Warts and EV thus provide the natural positive controls for high-burden, transcriptionally active cutaneous HPV infection.

Between asymptomatic carriage and frank lesion lies the most consequential and most contested role of beta-HPV: as a cofactor in the development of cSCC, the second most common human cancer. Beta-HPV is detected at high frequency in actinic keratoses (AK) and cSCC, particularly in organ-transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients, whose cSCC risk is elevated many-fold (Howley and Pfister 2015; Rollison, Viarisio, et al. 2019). The mechanistic model that reconciles this association with the virus’s commensal nature is the “hit-and-run” hypothesis: beta-HPV acts early, cooperating with ultraviolet (UV) radiation to expand a field of damaged keratinocytes, but is dispensable for maintenance of the established tumour. Beta-HPV E6 proteins impair the cellular response to UV damage, abrogating ATR signalling and the repair of UV-induced lesions, and disrupt NOTCH and TGF-β signalling to sustain proliferation, without degrading p53 as high-risk alpha-HPV does (Wallace et al. 2012; Meyers et al. 2017). Direct experimental support comes from transgenic and infection models in which genetic deletion of the viral oncogenes after lesions have formed, or transplantation of secondary tumours, leaves carcinoma growth unaffected and viral genomes undetectable (Viarisio et al. 2018; Dorfer et al. 2021), and from UV-dependent MmuPV1 skin carcinogenesis in mice (Uberoi et al. 2016). Consistent with hit-and-run, viral load and transcription in human tissue are highest in early precursor lesions and decline in established carcinoma (Borgogna et al. 2018). This view is not unchallenged. T-cell immunity to commensal papillomaviruses has been shown to be actively protective against skin carcinogenesis, reframing immunosuppression-associated cSCC as a failure of antiviral immunosurveillance rather than direct viral oncogenesis (Strickley et al. 2019); that claim drew a formal Matters Arising from the opposing camp and a reply (Lambert et al. 2021; Strickley et al. 2021), and the exchange remains unresolved. Two developments since have made the contest less tractable rather than more. First, the protective-immunity account now predicts the same longitudinal pattern as hit-and-run: in UV-damaged skin, papillomavirus colonisation blocks the expansion of mutant p53 clones in a CD8+ T-cell-dependent manner, beta-HPV activity is elevated in sun-exposed human skin carrying such clones, and the expansion of those clones in premalignant lesions is associated with loss of beta-HPV (Son et al. 2025). A decline in viral activity along the progression axis is therefore a prediction of both models, not a signature of either. Second, a purely virological explanation for quiescence exists alongside both: the beta-HPV genome represses its own gene expression and replication through the viral E8^E2 protein, and immortalisation of human keratinocytes by a beta-HPV genome requires that repressor to be inactivated (Rehm et al. 2022), so transcriptional quiet may be the cis-encoded default state of the virus rather than a statement about immunity or tumour biology. What is missing from this debate is not another mechanism but a measurement: how often, and how actively, cutaneous HPV is actually transcribed across the spectrum from healthy skin to carcinoma.

Resolving these questions requires distinguishing productive infection from latent, abortive, or transformed states, and the viral transcriptional programme provides exactly this readout. The papillomavirus life cycle is obligately coupled to keratinocyte differentiation: early genes (E1, E2, E5, E6, E7) are expressed in basal and proliferating cells, whereas genome amplification and the late capsid genes (L1, L2) are activated only in the terminally differentiated suprabasal layers, where virions are assembled and shed (Doorbar et al. 2012; Graham 2017). This temporal order is enforced by differentiation-dependent promoter switching, alternative splicing and a shift from early to late polyadenylation (Johansson and Schwartz 2013). Detection of late (L1/L2) capsid transcripts is consequently a hallmark of productive infection, and can be read out directly from RNA sequencing (Klymenko et al. 2017; Borgogna et al. 2014). The contrast is sharpest in cancer: when HPV integrates, the late programme, and frequently E2, is lost, leaving deregulated E6/E7 as the dominant viral transcripts (Moody and Laimins 2010). Integration itself is not a single state, and reading it from transcription rather than presence is what separates its variants: multi-omic profiling of cervical cancer distinguishes silent from productive integration sites by whether they generate viral-host fusion transcripts, finds only the productive class non-randomly distributed and associated with higher E6/E7 protein and more aggressive disease, and shows the productive fraction rising from carcinoma in situ to advanced disease (Fan et al. 2023). An early-versus-late transcript signature therefore separates the productive warts and EV lesions from the latent carriage of normal skin and from any non-productive footprint in carcinoma.

These questions are, in principle, already answerable from data that exist. Public sequence archives now hold millions of human RNA-seq libraries, and re-mining this resource has repeatedly recovered viral signal that the original studies ignored (Edgar et al. 2022). The obstacle is a near-universal feature of transcriptomic pipelines: reads that do not map to the human genome are discarded at the outset, so any HPV transcripts present are silently filtered away before analysis. Recovering them requires returning to the raw reads and classifying the non-human fraction explicitly, an approach validated by dedicated virus-detection workflows (Yasumizu et al. 2021) and efficient metagenomic classifiers such as Kraken2 (Wood, Lu, and Langmead 2019). Skin is no exception. Screening the off-target reads of commonly available sequencing data across 19 skin tumour types identified HPV42 as the driver of digital papillary adenocarcinoma, present in 96% of cases (Leiendecker et al. 2023), and a multidimensional reprocessing of 8,274 public skin RNA-seq samples from 132 experiments recovered bacterial, protist and viral RNA including HPV among the skin flora it catalogued (Bhargava et al. 2025). Neither discarded-read mining of skin nor its application at archive scale is therefore new; what has not been done is to use it to estimate how often cutaneous HPV is present, which types, and whether the infection is productive. Whether cutaneous HPV is transcriptionally active in skin cancer has in fact been asked directly, by several groups and on several platforms, and the answers converge. Transcriptome sequencing of cSCC concluded that HPV is “not active” in these tumours (Arron et al. 2011); total RNA sequencing of 12 skin lesions, 11 of them HPV DNA-positive, recovered transcripts from one, at a median of 66 million reads (Hultin et al. 2019); whole-transcriptome analysis of 345 post-transplant non-melanoma skin cancers at a median of 35 million reads found HPV transcription in 15 (Arroyo Mühr, Hultin, and Dillner 2021); RNA sequencing of 23 risk-stratified cSCC and normal-skin biopsies found no HPV expression at all, against 64% HPV DNA positivity in the same series (Vandiver et al. 2021); and E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization across 243 cutaneous SCC detected high-risk transcripts in 0.9% of the 225 non-anogenital cases (Fujimoto et al. 2019). The convergence is not total: an earlier in situ study found EV-HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant-recipient cSCC, localised to the mid and upper epidermis (Purdie et al. 2005), and whole-transcriptome virome profiling reads cutaneous HPV transcripts readily from EV skin (Saeidian et al. 2023). What no study has yet done is put the question on a denominator large enough, and a control series wide enough, to say what the population-level answer is: the transcriptomic series above run from 11 to 345 specimens, four of the five are confined to lesional tissue with no unselected-skin comparator, the largest is exclusively immunosuppressed and formalin-fixed, and the one covering the widest range of cutaneous types scores transcription of any viral gene rather than productive replication. The question is therefore not whether HPV transcripts can be found in cutaneous neoplasia, which is settled, but at what rate they occur across the skin spectrum, whether they represent productive infection, and how they compare with a lesion in which productive infection is certain. Any such effort must also contend with contamination: the HeLa cell line carries integrated HPV18 and is a pervasive source of spurious HPV18 (and HPV16/HPV38) reads in public datasets, propagated through shared reagents and index hopping (Cantalupo, Katz, and Pipas 2015; Kazemian et al. 2015; Adey et al. 2013). Distinguishing genuine infection from contaminant signal demands coverage-breadth and read-count thresholds, careful flagging of cell-line and engineered samples, and normalisation for sequencing depth so that apparent “burden” is not merely a function of how deeply a library was sequenced.

Here we systematically re-mine public human RNA-seq data to characterise the cutaneous HPV transcriptome across tissues and disease states, applying a uniform pipeline that screens every library for papillomavirus reads, types the positives against the full PaVE reference set, and classifies their early-versus-late transcriptional activity. We frame the analysis as a case/control design spanning productive controls (warts and EV), the unselected-skin null, and the open question of HPV-associated skin neoplasia (AK and cSCC), with cell-line and contamination signals identified and depth-normalised throughout. In doing so we address four questions: (1) which HPV types are prevalent in healthy human skin; (2) which HPV types are associated with the spectrum of skin pathology; (3) in which non-traditional tissues HPV transcripts can be detected; and (4) in which transcriptomes the virus reaches the productive (late-transcript) phase of its life cycle. The first and third of these have been answered at DNA level, by body-site metagenomic mapping of healthy carriage (Ma et al. 2014); what is asked here is the transcriptional counterpart, which is a different quantity and, as the results show, a much smaller one.

Methods

Overview and implementation

All analyses were performed with a custom, portable workflow implemented in Nextflow DSL2 (≥23.04; Di Tommaso et al. (2017)) and run on an HPC cluster under the SLURM scheduler. Each step runs in an isolated, version-pinned software environment specified per process as both a Conda environment.yml and an OCI container image; the exact container build was used for execution, and the versions quoted below are those pinned by the container tags. Default parameter values are given in parentheses and were used unless stated otherwise.

The workflow comprises a one-time reference-construction stage followed by a per-sample pipeline: SRA discovery → FASTQ download → quality control → Kraken2 papillomavirus screen → branch on HPV status (only HPV-positive libraries proceed) → STAR alignment to the HPV reference panel → coverage-based HPV typing → early/late transcript classification → aggregation and reporting.

HPV reference panel and Kraken2 database

A cutaneous-inclusive HPV reference panel was assembled from the Papillomavirus Episteme (PaVE 2.0; Van Doorslaer et al. (2017)). Because PaVE 2.0 exposes no bulk-FASTA endpoint, genomes were enumerated through its REST API (GET /api/genome?limit=9999&includeNonRef=true, which includes non-reference candidate genomes), filtered to human-host entries (host_common_name == "human"), and retrieved individually (GET /api/genome/{locus_id}), with each genome sequence taken from the returned itemSequence. Reference-quality complete HPV genomes from NCBI RefSeq were added on a best-effort basis via Entrez Direct (≥16.2; "Human papillomavirus"[Organism] AND refseq[filter] AND complete genome[Title]). Sequences were concatenated and deduplicated by identifier (seqkit ≥2.5; W. Shen et al. (2016)) to yield the final panel (hpv_all.fasta; n = 455 genomes spanning the alpha, beta, gamma, mu and nu genera plus unclassified candidate types; the panel is built at setup from live PaVE/RefSeq queries and its exact composition depends on build date). A per-type genus lookup was derived from the PaVE ICTV taxonomy array. Gene models for the eight protein-coding ORFs of interest (E1, E2, E4, E5, E6, E7, L1, L2) were extracted from each genome’s PaVE feature annotation, with multi-segment features collapsed to a single span, and written as a GFF3 annotation used downstream for transcript classification.

A STAR genome index was built over the panel (STAR ≥2.7.10; --genomeSAindexNbases 6 for the small viral genomes). A Kraken2 database (≥2.1.3; Wood, Lu, and Langmead (2019)) was constructed from the NCBI taxonomy and the human reference library (GRCh38), to which all panel HPV genomes were added under a Papillomaviridae taxon, so that human and HPV reads are jointly classified and HPV reads are resolved within the papillomavirus clade.

Dataset assembly and SRA discovery

Public human RNA-seq libraries were identified by programmatic query of the NCBI Sequence Read Archive through Entrez (Biopython Bio.Entrez; pysradb/Biopython container 2.2.1), with every query intersected with a common base filter ("Homo sapiens"[Organism] AND "RNA-Seq"[Strategy] AND "public"[Access]). We used three complementary discovery strategies, corresponding to the case/control framing of the study. An unbiased prevalence sweep of human skin and related tissues (the prevalence cohort) estimated baseline HPV-positivity rates in tissue not selected for infection. A targeted productive-lesion query (epidermodysplasia verruciformis, verruca/warts, condyloma) provided positive controls of known productive cutaneous HPV infection. A broadened skin-neoplasia query additionally captured cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis and Bowen disease alongside the wider wart/papilloma vocabulary, to interrogate HPV across the AK-to-cSCC setting.

For each retrieved run, metadata were parsed into a per-run samplesheet (one row per SRR). A tissue category was assigned by longest-keyword-first matching of sample title and source fields against a curated keyword table, yielding one of four classes: skin, anogenital, oral, or unclassified (the default, meaning no site keyword was present rather than a site outside the other three). Keywords are matched with letter boundaries on both sides, tolerating a plural suffix, so that a keyword is not matched inside an unrelated word; the boundary is letter-based rather than word-based because SRA free text routinely separates tokens with underscores and digits. Squamous- and basal-cell-carcinoma abbreviations are exempt from the boundary rule, since they legitimately take anatomical affixes (cSCC, RDEB-SCC, SCCIS). A free-text diagnosis was extracted against a fixed pathology vocabulary (carcinoma, SCC, BCC, keratosis, wart, verruca, condyloma, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, dysplasia/CIN, normal/healthy/control, and similar terms), defaulting to “unspecified”. Library layout (single- vs paired-end) was taken from the SRA record. To enable robust downstream parsing, comma-containing free-text fields were retained in a raw samplesheet and stripped from the slim samplesheet consumed by the workflow.

Read download and quality control

FASTQ files were retrieved from the SRA (Leinonen, Sugawara, and Shumway 2011) with the NCBI SRA Toolkit (3.1.1, pinned; later 3.4.x builds were unstable in our environment) by prefetch followed by fasterq-dump --split-3, and compressed with pigz. Reads were quality- and adapter-trimmed with fastp (0.23.4; Chen et al. (2018)) using a minimum qualified base quality of Phred 20 (--qualified_quality_phred 20) and a minimum retained read length of 36 nt (--length_required 36); paired-end libraries additionally used --detect_adapter_for_pe. Per-sample failures (withdrawn accessions, network errors) were tolerated by a fail-soft retry-then-ignore policy so that a single unavailable run did not abort a batch. Every library was screened in full: no step subsamples reads, and fasterq-dump was run without a spot limit. This matters more than it may appear, because reads deposited from a coordinate-sorted alignment emerge from the SRA in reference order, which places unmapped, and therefore viral, reads at the end of the run; screening only the leading portion of such a library would miss the signal entirely and would do so non-randomly. As a check on the whole path from download to classification, the reads reaching the Kraken2 screen correspond to a median 98.6% of the SRA-reported spot count across the 10,849 screened libraries (5th percentile 85.5%), the small shortfall being fastp quality and length filtering, and the per-tier medians span 95.8% to 100%, so no population tier was read less completely than another.

HPV screening and positivity calling

Trimmed reads were classified against the combined human+HPV Kraken2 database (≥2.1.3, paired or single mode as appropriate). HPV-classified reads were enumerated as the count of unique read identifiers assigned to the Papillomaviridae family or any papillomavirus genus/type taxon. A library was called HPV-positive when its HPV read count met or exceeded a threshold of 10 reads (hpv_min_reads = 10), and HPV-negative otherwise; HPV-negative libraries were recorded for rate estimation but proceeded no further. HPV-classified reads from positive libraries were extracted (seqtk 1.4), keeping paired mates in register, for targeted alignment. This split, in which every screened library contributes to positivity rates but only positives advance to typing, is the central branch point of the workflow.

HPV typing

HPV reads from positive libraries were aligned to the HPV reference panel with STAR (2.7.11b; Dobin et al. (2013)) in an end-to-end, splice-disabled configuration appropriate for compact viral genomes (--alignIntronMax 1, --alignEndsType EndToEnd, --outFilterMismatchNmax 3), permitting up to 50 multi-mapping locations (--outFilterMultimapNmax 50) to accommodate the high sequence similarity among HPV types. Sorted, indexed BAMs were summarised per reference with samtools coverage (samtools 1.21; Danecek et al. (2021)) at a minimum mapping quality of 10. For each reference we recorded read count, covered bases, coverage breadth (fraction of the reference covered ≥1×) and mean depth. A reference was assigned to a sample when it satisfied both coverage breadth ≥ 0.10 (hpv_min_coverage) and mean depth ≥ 2 (hpv_min_depth); the full per-reference coverage table was retained regardless of assignment. The dual breadth-and-depth criterion guards against spurious assignment from a few reads piling up on a short, conserved region.

Early/late transcript classification

To distinguish productive from non-productive infection, reads from each HPV-positive alignment were assigned to viral genes with featureCounts (subread ≥2.0; Liao, Smyth, and Shi (2014)) against the PaVE-derived gene annotation (-t gene -g gene_name, minimum overlap 20 nt, minimum mapping quality 10; pairing detected directly from the BAM and counted as read pairs when applicable). Per-gene counts were aggregated into an early total (E1, E2, E4, E5, E6, E7) and a late total (L1, L2). An infection was classified as productive when the L1 (major-capsid) read count reached the late-transcript threshold of 3 (late_transcript_min_reads = 3). Productivity was gated on L1 specifically, rather than on combined L1+L2 signal, because L1 capsid expression is the more stringent marker of virion-producing late-stage infection, whereas isolated L2 signal can arise from low-level transcription or cross-mapping; this single rule was applied uniformly across all samples and run batches.

Cell-line, engineered, and contaminant flagging

Because public RNA-seq is heavily populated by cancer cell lines, many carrying integrated HPV (e.g. HeLa/HPV18) that is a well-documented source of spurious HPV signal in archived data (Cantalupo, Katz, and Pipas 2015; Kazemian et al. 2015), every sample was annotated along three independent axes from its metadata using a shared pattern library: is_cell_line (named lines such as HeLa, SiHa, CaSki, HaCaT, A431, plus generic markers like “cell line”, “immortalized”, “passage n”, ATCC/DSMZ accessioning, PDX/xenograft), is_engineered (shRNA/siRNA/sgRNA, CRISPR/Cas9, transduction/transfection, lentiviral and plasmid-backbone constructs), and is_in_vitro (cultured but non-immortalised material such as primary keratinocytes/fibroblasts/melanocytes, NHEK, organotypic/raft cultures, organoids, and differentiation time-courses). Explicit “primary” annotations were treated as non-cell-line. These flags annotate rather than exclude samples, so that cell-line positives are retained as positive controls but can be separated from primary-tissue signal at analysis. For the prevalence-sweep cohort, study-level heuristic calls were additionally refined by manual curation through a structured workbook, with precedence sample > study > heuristic, and a provenance label recorded for each overridden call. As a further contaminant guard, low-coverage-breadth assignments (breadth < 0.15) and alpha-genus/HPV16/HPV18 calls were tabulated by study to surface project-level contamination.

Cohort framing and depth-normalised burden analysis

Because lesional libraries may simply be sequenced more deeply than unselected skin, raw HPV read counts confound infection burden with sequencing depth. To neutralise this, every Kraken2-screened library, including HPV-negative ones, was scored as papillomavirus reads per million (RPM), computed from the Kraken2 report as the Papillomaviridae clade read count divided by the sum of unclassified and root-level clade reads, times 10⁶. Samples were assigned to mutually exclusive population tiers in fixed precedence: cell_line (any cell-line flag), EV (epidermodysplasia verruciformis diagnosis), control_productive (wart/condyloma), neoplasia (squamous/carcinoma/SCC/keratosis/Bowen), contamination_study (pre-specified contaminated studies), unselected_skin (skin tissue), and other.

Because these rules read free-text SRA metadata, they mis-file the minority of studies whose submitted metadata is absent or actively misleading. Four such cases were identified by inspecting every library that reached the detection floor, and corrected through a curated override table (assets/tier_overrides.csv) in which each row records the accession, the corrected field, and the evidence. (i) A ten-library cohort of epidermodysplasia verruciformis patient skin biopsies (Saeidian et al. 2023) carries only tissue=Skin in its per-run metadata, so the diagnosis vocabulary never sees “verruciformis”; these were moved to the EV tier, which otherwise contained only immortalised EV culture models (retained under cell_line). (ii) Fifteen libraries annotated source_name=Skin or mucosa, tissue=adjacent mucosal tissues are the matched peri-lesional tissue of five condyloma acuminatum donors whose lesions are themselves in control_productive; the tissue matcher had filed them as skin on the substring “Skin”. They were placed in a separate peri_lesional tier, since neither an unselected-skin null nor a productive control describes them. (iii) Six libraries from a study of HPV31-positive HaCaT (HaCaT31) cells expose only a knockdown label and skin in their parsed fields, so no cell-line pattern can fire; the cell-line flag was set. (iv) One primary cutaneous wart carried a submitter sample label in the SRA cell_line attribute and was wrongly flagged as a line; the flag was cleared, returning it to control_productive. Together these corrections move 31 of 11,282 libraries. The same is_cell_line corrections are applied to the positivity model, so that sample-class definitions are identical across models. Running the pipeline with the override table disabled reproduces the uncorrected tier assignment exactly, and both outputs are retained. A control-calibrated detection floor was defined as the 5th-percentile RPM of non-cell-line productive controls (warts/condyloma); libraries below this floor were considered “not detected at control level”. To show that any tier difference was not an artefact of depth, the fraction of libraries at or above the detection floor was additionally computed within matched total-read bins (<5M, 5–10M, 10–20M, 20–40M, >40M). The same per-sample table also yielded an HPV-type × tier catalogue. This analysis pooled the lesion cohorts against the prevalence-sweep null and used the curated cell-line flags. Logistic-regression models (positivity by sample class; productive-level detection by tier with a log10 sequencing-depth covariate) and Fisher exact tests were fitted in R; Wilson intervals are reported for proportions. As a robustness check, the positivity, depth-controlled detection and productivity models were additionally refitted as Bayesian logistic regressions with explicit weakly-informative priors, namely Normal(0, 2.5) on the log-odds coefficients and Normal(0, 5) on the intercept, applied directly to the log-odds scale rather than as flat or improper defaults, using rstanarm (Goodrich et al. 2024) (four Markov chains of 2,000 iterations; convergence confirmed by \(\hat{R} \le 1.004\) with no divergent transitions). Effects are summarised by the posterior median odds ratio, its 95% credible interval, and the posterior probability of a positive effect; the near-separated productive-controls-versus-skin contrast was additionally checked under a heavier-tailed Student-t(3) prior (Table S3).

Library-selection chemistry

Sequencing depth bounds what a viral-transcript survey can detect, and RNA-selection chemistry bounds it in a second, independent way: poly-A capture recovers polyadenylated early transcripts efficiently but is inefficient for the rest of the viral pool, so two libraries of equal depth need not have equal power to detect HPV. Chemistry was therefore looked up for every library in the burden analysis and entered alongside depth. SRA RunInfo LibrarySelection was fetched for the exact accession set already analysed, with no fresh search, so the cohort is unchanged (bin/fetch_library_selection.py). That field is authoritative where it carries a specific value (“PolyA”, “Oligo-dT”, “Inverse rRNA”, “RANDOM”) but is the generic “cDNA” for 74.7% of libraries, so the free-text LIBRARY_CONSTRUCTION_PROTOCOL and DESIGN_DESCRIPTION records were fetched in a second pass and matched against curated poly-A and rRNA-depletion phrase sets (bin/classify_library_chemistry.py). Libraries whose text supports both calls, or neither, are held at unspecified rather than assigned, and the amplification chemistries that are neither selection (3’-barcoded droplet libraries, SMART template-switching) are kept as their own levels rather than pooled with poly-A capture. This resolved chemistry for 6,751 of 10,849 libraries (62.2%).

The two-source procedure is necessary rather than merely convenient, and the graded cervical validation series is the demonstration: every one of its libraries is filed in SRA as LibrarySelection = cDNA, while its construction protocol reads “Ribosomal RNA was deleted”. Run as a blind test, the classifier recovers rRNA depletion for 15/15 of them from protocol text alone, which is also the independent confirmation that the series is rRNA-depleted rather than poly-A-selected.

Integration status: E1:E2 transcript ratio and virus–host junctions

Integration of a papillomavirus genome disrupts the E2 open reading frame, which represses E6 and E7. Because E1 and E2 are encoded on the same early transcript, their read counts track one another unless that disruption has occurred, so their ratio reports integration from the transcript classification already computed for every library. Libraries with at least five combined E1 and E2 reads were scored as log2((E1 + 0.5)/(E2 + 0.5)); separation between tiers was quantified as the area under the ranked ratio and by Wilcoxon rank-sum test. A ratio is undefined where integration has proceeded to the point that the early region is lost apart from E6 and E7, since E1 and E2 are then both silent. Those libraries were called by a second criterion: at least five combined E6 and E7 reads, fewer than five combined E1 and E2 reads, and no more than 5% of viral reads assigned to L1 or L2, which is the integrated-carcinoma pattern of oncogene transcription without a late programme. A library was called integration-like if either criterion fired; the two are reported separately because the first is blind to the material the second detects.

The ratio was validated against direct evidence of integration in a subset of 17 libraries spanning its range. Reads were aligned with STAR (Dobin et al. 2013) to a combined index of GRCh38 and the HPV reference panel, with chimeric detection enabled (--chimSegmentMin 20, --chimJunctionOverhangMin 15), and chimeric junctions were retained when one side fell on an HPV contig and the other on a human chromosome. Integration was scored not by the number of such junctions, which scales with viral depth and is largest in episomal libraries, but by their clustering: the fraction of a library’s junctions falling at its single most-supported coordinate pair, since a genuine integration yields one recurrent junction whereas chimeric-read artefacts are scattered. Observed values were bimodal with an empty interval between 0.00–0.03 and 0.33–0.46, and a threshold of 0.2 was placed within it. The limit of a negative call was set empirically rather than by model: integration was called in a library carrying as few as 2,776 HPV reads, which bounds the viral depth at which absence is informative.

The ratio was validated externally on a graded cervical series (BioProject PRJNA612785, study SRP252916): HPV-negative normal cervical epithelium, HPV16-positive normal epithelium, HPV16-positive high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and HPV16-positive squamous carcinoma, six cases per arm, all paired-end and rRNA-depleted rather than poly(A)-selected. Libraries were typed with the same pipeline and scored with the same criteria and thresholds as the skin cohort, with the study’s own design arms supplied in place of the tier assignment (bin/e1e2_integration_marker.R --groups), so the marker was evaluated against labels it had no part in assigning. Single-cell and single-nucleus libraries are excluded from the marker by default throughout, since 3’-biased barcoded coverage cannot support a ratio across the early region; truncating such libraries does not remedy this, so they are dropped rather than downsampled.

Execution at scale

For cohorts of thousands of libraries, a chunked driver processed the samplesheet in fixed-size batches (default 100 libraries per chunk). After each successful chunk, per-sample outputs (Kraken2 reports, HPV typing and transcript tables, and HPV status) were aggregated and the chunk’s working directory was deleted to bound disk use; a failed chunk was left intact for inspection and resumed on rerun. A single combined report was generated over the aggregated outputs at completion. Summary tables and figures were produced in R (tidyverse), and the depth-normalised burden analysis was implemented as a standalone R script operating on the aggregated Kraken2 reports, typing tables, and curated sample flags.

Code and data availability

The complete analysis pipeline, comprising the Nextflow workflow, the per-process software environments and container definitions, the reference-construction and SRA-discovery scripts, and the downstream R analysis and statistical-inference code, is openly available at https://github.com/tpall/hpv-human-skin. All sequencing data analysed here are public and were obtained from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive; the per-cohort lists of accessions (SRR/SRX), with assigned tissue category, diagnosis, and cell-line/engineered annotations, are provided as Supplementary Data. Reference genomes were retrieved from the Papillomavirus Episteme (PaVE; https://pave.niaid.nih.gov) and NCBI RefSeq.

Results

We screened public human RNA-seq libraries for papillomavirus reads under three discovery strategies (Methods): an unbiased prevalence sweep of skin and related tissues (11,556 libraries screened), a targeted query of productive cutaneous lesions providing positive controls (53 wart/epidermodysplasia-verruciformis skin libraries), and a broadened skin-neoplasia sweep capturing cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), actinic keratosis (AK) and Bowen disease (1,070 libraries screened). Throughout, every screened library, including HPV-negative ones, was scored as papillomavirus reads per million (RPM) so that infection burden could be separated from sequencing depth, and each sample was annotated as primary tissue, cell line, or engineered material.

HPV signal in public RNA-seq is dominated by cell-line and engineered artefacts

In the unbiased sweep, HPV positivity was strongly concentrated in non-primary material. Engineered libraries were HPV-positive in 9.28% of cases (95% CI 5.95–14.19) and cell-line libraries in 10.34% (7.76–13.63), versus only 2.13% (1.87–2.42) of clinical primary-tissue libraries (Table 1). In logistic regression this corresponded to roughly five-fold higher odds of positivity for engineered (OR 4.7, 95% CI 2.8–7.8, P = 1.5×10⁻⁹) and cell-line (OR 5.3, 3.8–7.5, P = 9.9×10⁻²²) samples relative to clinical tissue (likelihood-ratio P = 8.5×10⁻²⁰). These positives were almost entirely the high-risk mucosal alpha types: HPV18 accounted for 32/34 of its calls in cell lines and HPV16 for 24/28 (Table S1), the expected signature of integrated-HPV cell lines such as HeLa and of their well-documented cross-contamination of archived sequencing data. Genuine primary skin therefore carries HPV at a low rate (2–4%, below), and the apparent abundance of HPV in public transcriptomes is largely a laboratory artefact that must be partitioned out before any prevalence claim.

The transcripts themselves carry an independent signature of that artefact, in two forms. E1 and E2 are encoded on the same early polycistronic message, so their read counts should track one another; integration characteristically disrupts the E2 open reading frame while sparing E1, inverting the ratio. Cell-line libraries show a median E1:E2 of 129, against 0.27 in productive controls, 0.49 in unselected skin and 0.04 in neoplasia, and the ratio separates cell lines from productive primary infection almost completely (AUC 0.97, Wilcoxon P = 2.8×10⁻¹⁴; Figure 1 A). Where integration has gone further and the early region is lost but for E6 and E7, both E1 and E2 fall silent and no ratio can be formed; those libraries instead show oncogene transcription with no late transcription at all, the canonical integrated-carcinoma pattern, and are captured by that criterion. Together the two signatures call 89.2% of 93 cell-line libraries as integration-like (41 by the inverted ratio, 42 by the E6/E7-only pattern the ratio cannot see) while calling 0% of EV biopsies and 0% of peri-lesional mucosa, the two tiers where infection is episomal by definition. That it reports integration rather than culture is settled by the one cell line in the cohort that maintains its genome episomally, an HPV31-positive HaCaT derivative, which sits at 0.6–1.0 alongside primary tissue rather than with the integrated lines. Applied as a detector, the ratio flags 33 libraries that carry the integration signature without being labelled as cell lines, including melanoma lines under shRNA knockdown recorded with a tissue source of “skin” and cutaneous SCC lines recorded with a carcinoma diagnosis, which is what motivates the engineered tier above. The ratio was checked against the event it claims to report. Calling virus–host chimeric reads against a combined human/HPV index in 17 libraries spanning the range of the ratio separates the same groups completely (Figure 1 B), provided integration is scored as a recurrent junction rather than a raw count: the fraction of a library’s junctions falling at its single most-supported site is 0.33–0.46 where the ratio indicates integration and 0.00–0.03 where it does not, with no overlap. Raw counts are misleading in the opposite direction, since the two epidermodysplasia-verruciformis libraries generate the largest number of junctions in the panel while being episomal. The positive controls recover the expected answer unprompted: 5 of 5 cell-line libraries are integration-positive, and two independently return the same junction at chromosome 8q24, the documented integration site of the HeLa lineage.

The ratio was then read against a progression in which the answer is known independently. A cervical series (SRP252916) sequenced HPV16-positive normal epithelium, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and squamous carcinoma, six cases per arm under one rRNA-depleted protocol, alongside six HPV-negative normal controls; the arms are the submitting study’s, and the tissue and the progression are ones the marker was not developed on. The HPV-negative controls returned no HPV of any type, and across the three positive arms the median E1:E2 rises monotonically with grade, from -1.48 in normal epithelium (n = 3) through -0.36 in HSIL (n = 6) to 1.47 in carcinoma (n = 6), a shift of roughly eightfold in the direction integration predicts (Figure 1 C). Late transcription tracks the same axis without being part of the criterion: the libraries called episomal carry abundant L1, while those with a disrupted ratio carry almost none. The binary call is the weaker readout at this size, separating the carcinoma and lesion arms from normal epithelium (2 and 2 of six against 0 of 3) but not from each other, and the normal-epithelium arm is thin: two of its six libraries yielded no HPV reads and a third carried two. The gradient, not the threshold, is what this series supports.

Skin neoplasia carries only trace HPV, not productive infection, and this is not a depth artefact

The central question, whether HPV is transcriptionally active in cSCC/AK or present only as a residual footprint, was resolved by the depth-normalised burden analysis (Figure 2). Productive controls (warts/condyloma) were detected at or above the control-calibrated detection floor (13.2 RPM) in 93.2% of libraries, with a median burden of 5,408 RPM; the EV biopsy tier, sequenced most deeply of all (median 62.6M reads), reached it in 80% (median 229.6 RPM). In stark contrast, the neoplasia tier reached this floor in only 1.5% of libraries (median 0.012 RPM), six orders of magnitude below the productive controls, despite being sequenced almost four times more deeply than they were (median 45.2M vs 12.2M reads). Unselected skin, once the peri-lesional and EV material that the targeted queries had swept into it was reassigned to its own tiers (Methods), forms an almost clean null: 0.1% of 7,800 libraries reach the floor.

This gap is not explained by sequencing depth. Modelling productive-level detection (RPM ≥ floor) as a function of population tier and log sequencing depth, productive controls exceeded unselected skin by close to four orders of magnitude (Fisher exact OR 10,183, 95% CI 3,250 to ∞ under separation, P = 7.6×10⁻⁹⁹), while neoplasia sat an order of magnitude above skin (OR 14, 95% CI 4.5–46, P = 6.7×10⁻⁶). That contrast is easier to read on the absolute scale from which the odds ratios derive: 41/44 productive controls cross the floor, against 6/406 neoplasia libraries and 7/7,800 skin libraries. Neoplasia is thus measurably, but marginally, above a near-zero baseline, and remains roughly 62-fold below the productive controls in detection rate.

Crucially, that marginal excess is not productive burden, and it is not bought by depth. Sequencing depth raised the odds of detecting any HPV read (OR per log₁₀ reads 5.2, 4.6–5.9, P = 5.1×10⁻¹⁴⁴), but it did not raise the odds of reaching the detection floor, either as a covariate across tiers (OR 1.5, 0.4–5.2, P = 0.49) or within the neoplasia tier alone (OR 1.6, 95% CI 0.1–19, P = 0.7). The deepest cSCC/AK libraries, at 327.3M reads, did not cross the productive floor. Consistent with a residual footprint rather than active infection, neoplasia showed a clear excess of trace HPV (any read; OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.6–2.4, P = 5.5×10⁻¹⁰ vs unselected skin) alongside its small floor-level excess, but neither amounted to productive burden. The depth-matched detection profile confirms the same pattern non-parametrically: across every sequencing-depth bin, productive controls detect at 90–100% while neoplasia and unselected skin stay near zero (Figure S1). At population scale, then, HPV in cutaneous neoplasia is a low-level, transcriptionally inactive trace, the signature predicted by the hit-and-run model, and not the productive infection seen in warts. That trace is also not integrated virus, which the junction analysis measures rather than infers: of 6 HPV-positive cSCC/AK libraries carrying enough viral reads to test, 4 show no integration junction at all, and the 2 that do are HPV16 libraries the broadened query swept in from mucosal disease (Table S4), where integration is the expected state. The negatives are not limited by viral depth: integration was called in a library carrying only 2,776 HPV reads, and every junction-negative cSCC library exceeds that by at least 3.9-fold.

Nor is it explained by how the libraries were built. Depth is one bound on viral-transcript recovery; RNA-selection chemistry is the other, and poly-A capture is the chemistry least favourable to it. Chemistry was resolved for 6,751 libraries (62.2%) from SRA metadata and library-construction protocol text, and it is not balanced across tiers, but the imbalance runs against the negative result rather than producing it: the neoplasia tier is rRNA-depleted in 22.9% of libraries against 7.2% of unselected skin, while the productive controls, the tier in which productive infection is abundant, contain no rRNA-depleted libraries at all. The tier in which no productive infection is found was thus built, three times more often than its comparator, with the chemistry most favourable to finding it. Within the two tiers of the contrast, and adjusting for depth and tier, rRNA-depleted libraries were no more likely than poly-A libraries to carry any HPV read (OR 1.0, 95% CI 0.8–1.2, P = 0.93; OR 1.2, 1.0–1.4 across all tiers). What did move trace detection, by three- to four-fold at equal depth, was not selection chemistry but amplification: SMART template-switching (OR 4.4) and 3’-barcoded droplet libraries (OR 3.6), a pattern that reads as amplification and barcode-swapping artefact rather than recovery. Adding chemistry to the models leaves both contrasts intact (trace OR 2.0, P = 8.7×10⁻¹¹; floor-level OR 14, P = 1.7×10⁻⁵). The decisive test is to discard the ambiguity and use only the favourable chemistry: among the 657 rRNA-depleted libraries in the contrast (564 skin, 93 neoplasia from 3 studies, median 45.6M and deepest 96.8M reads), the trace excess in neoplasia is larger still (OR 5.6, 3.4–9.2, P = 7.2×10⁻¹²) and not one library, in either tier, reached the productive floor.

Pooling actinic keratosis with carcinoma is a choice the data support rather than an assumption. Split on diagnosis, the tier comprises 72 AK libraries from 6 studies and 326 cSCC libraries from 19 studies (a further 8 naming both are held out as ambiguous). Both arms sit well above unselected skin, and by almost identical margins: trace HPV at OR 2.6 for AK (P = 1.5×10⁻⁴) and OR 1.9 for cSCC (P = 5.6×10⁻⁸), and productive-floor detection at OR 14 and 14. Against each other they are indistinguishable on either measure, depth-adjusted: trace OR 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.3, P = 0.28), and floor-level detection 1/72 against 5/326 (Fisher P = 1). The precursor lesion and the carcinoma carry the same trace, non-productive HPV signal, so the tier is not averaging two different phenomena.

The transcript programme itself makes the distinction visible (Figure 3). Read gene by gene, the productive tiers run the complete viral programme, capsid genes included: 90% of productive-control libraries and 95.5% of EV biopsies carry L1 reads. Skin and neoplasia are not a truncated version of that programme but a uniformly faint one, low across the whole genome alike (unselected skin 10.3% for E6 and 18.6% for L1), which is the signature of a trace rather than of a life cycle arrested before its late phase. Cell lines are the third shape and the one that matters for provenance: E6 and E7 in 90.4% and 93.4% of libraries against E2 in 33.8% and L2 in 10.6%, the integrated pattern of Figure 1 generalised from one ratio to the whole genome. Where there are enough reads to apportion, the same contrast appears as composition: productive controls place 34.9% of their viral reads on the late genes against 6.4% on E6 and E7, and cell lines invert this exactly, 2.2% late against 66.6% oncogenic.

Tissue that cannot host the virus fixes the meaning of that trace. Papillomaviruses replicate only in differentiating stratified squamous epithelium, so cutaneous adipose, blood and neural material offer no permissive compartment at all; the 334 such libraries nonetheless carried a trace HPV read at 28.7%, indistinguishable from the 28% of unselected skin, while 0% reached the detection floor and not one yielded a single assignable HPV type. The background rate of trace HPV reads is therefore not a measure of infection: it is the assay’s floor, reproduced at the same level in tissue where infection is biologically impossible. Read against that control, the trace signal in unselected skin and in neoplasia is what a library returns when no productive infection is present.

Most of the small floor-level excess is in fact attributable to a handful of libraries the broadened SCC/CIN query captured: 3 of the 6 above-floor neoplasia libraries are high-risk mucosal HPV16 cases in squamous-cell carcinoma, conservatively retained in the neoplasia tier (Table S4). Excluding them halves the effect, lowering cutaneous-neoplasia floor-level detection to 0.7% (OR vs skin 7.5, P = 0.0055) and strengthening the productivity contrast against warts/EV (OR 5.2, P = 0.0038), so the retained tier is the conservative choice.

The assay detects bona fide productive cutaneous HPV, including genuine infections in primary skin

That the trace neoplasia signal reflects biology rather than assay insensitivity is established by the positive controls, which the pipeline detects robustly. Among targeted wart/EV libraries, 64% (34/53) met the strict productive criterion (≥3 L1 major-capsid reads), spanning the classic cutaneous repertoire: wart-associated alpha types (HPV2, HPV27, HPV57), low-risk mucocutaneous types (HPV6, HPV11), and beta/gamma types (Table S1). Productive infection was significantly more frequent in these controls than among HPV-positive neoplasia libraries (32%, 7/22; Fisher exact OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.2–13, P = 0.013).

Even so, a minority of genuine, non-cell-line skin lesions did harbour unambiguous productive infection, showing that the trace-level population result does not exclude real cutaneous HPV disease. The strongest cases were a cSCC skin library productively infected with the gamma-type HPV12 (99.8% genome coverage; L1 = 1,803, L2 = 3,546 reads), two HPV16-productive cSCC libraries, and two libraries from cutaneous actinic-keratosis/cSCC cohorts whose SRA records carry no tissue field (an actinic keratosis and a carcinoma) co-infected with the gamma types HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage (98–99%) and high depth (60–245×), with hundreds of L1 and L2 reads each (Table S2). These represent the answer to the productive-infection question: bona fide, high-confidence productive beta/gamma-HPV infections do occur in primary skin and skin-associated lesions, but they are the exception against a null background. They do not answer the non-traditional-tissue question, because the residual tier that would have to supply that evidence is defined by the absence of a site keyword rather than by an identified non-cutaneous site: the two co-infected libraries above sit there only because their cutaneous cohorts record no tissue field at all.

The HPV type landscape is partitioned by population

The HPV-type-by-tier catalogue (Table S1) recapitulates these conclusions in a single descriptive view, and the corrected tiering sharpens it. The high-risk mucosal types HPV16/HPV18 are confined almost entirely to cell-line material (3.5% [2.3–5.0] and 4.7% [3.2–6.3] of cell-line libraries). Productive controls are dominated by cutaneous wart types (HPV57, HPV2, HPV27) plus the low-risk mucocutaneous HPV6/HPV11 and gamma types (HPV4, HPV-mKN1). The EV tier carries precisely the beta-types the syndrome is defined by (HPV9, HPV14, HPV20, HPV25, HPV47) alongside an alpha co-detection. Peri-lesional mucosa carries the mucosal alpha repertoire of its adjacent condylomata (HPV11 in 91% [73–99] of libraries, HPV42, HPV6, HPV74, HPV90). Unselected skin, by contrast, contributes no HPV type at all above the two-library display threshold except two HPV18 contamination calls: its beta/gamma reservoir is real but sits entirely below the assignment threshold, and is recovered only at the detection tier (below). The genuine neoplasia-associated productive infections are the gamma/alpha types noted above (HPV12, HPV16, HPV96, HPV182). Collapsed from type to genus (Figure 4), the same partition is a single picture: productive controls are alpha with a gamma minority, EV biopsies are essentially pure beta (10/10 libraries), peri-lesional mucosa is purely alpha, cell lines are alpha, and unselected skin is flat and low across alpha, beta and gamma, with the study’s only nu detections. Cutaneous neoplasia is the one tissue tier in which beta exceeds alpha (2.8% [1.4–4.6] versus 2.1% [0.94–3.7]), the genus-level shadow of a beta-HPV footprint. The epidemiological reservoir of cutaneous beta/gamma HPV in healthy skin is therefore real but transcriptionally quiet, productive disease is the property of warts and EV, and HPV-associated cutaneous neoplasia carries the virus, when at all, as a trace, non-productive footprint.

Extending this catalogue below the assignment threshold answers the descriptive question of which types make up the trace. A detection-tier re-map of the HPV-positive but untyped libraries, taking the best-hit reference from unique alignments at sub-threshold coverage, resolved a confident low-coverage type for 137 of 325 such libraries across 42 types (Table S6). This recovers the expected commensal signal at the sensitivity floor: healthy skin carried a diverse cutaneous reservoir (40 of 51 resolved skin calls were beta-, gamma- or nu-types, including HPV12/HPV20, HPV4/HPV65/HPV134 and candidate skin-virome types), cutaneous neoplasia the carcinoma-associated beta and gamma types (HPV5, HPV12, HPV182, HPV222), while the mucosal HPV16/HPV18 signal stayed confined to cell-line material and a low-level contamination overlay. These are low-coverage, non-productive detections that identify the type without bearing on productivity, and so extend the type catalogue rather than qualify the trace-not-productive conclusion.

A further descriptive feature of the catalogue is that types frequently co-occur: 38 of the 163 typed libraries carry two or more assigned references, up to five in one library (Table S7). Because coverage is scored from uniquely-mapped reads alone, cross-mapping between similar types cannot generate these calls. The commonest pairing by far is HPV11 with HPV42, which co-occur in 20 libraries, while only 2 carry HPV42 without HPV11; in the peri-lesional tier the pairing is forced by the marginal counts of Table S1 (14 HPV11 and 13 HPV42 calls over 15 libraries). We nonetheless present this as a hypothesis rather than a finding, for three reasons set out in Table S7. The co-infected libraries are heavily pseudo-replicated, 25 of the 38 coming from 9 donors of one study, each sequenced in three fractions across two SRA submissions; the secondary type in a co-infection is usually near the detection threshold (median depth 6.8×, 40% below 5×), to the point that one donor’s MeRIP input and IP fractions call different second types; and requiring both partners to clear a stricter coverage bar leaves only 9 HPV11/HPV42 libraries from 3 donors. Within that stricter set the deeper type differs by tissue, HPV11 in the condyloma lesion and HPV42 in the two peri-lesional specimens, but HPV42 clears the bar only where it is abundant, so tissue tropism and detection sensitivity are confounded. The pattern is worth testing in a cohort assembled for the purpose; it cannot be resolved here.

A Bayesian re-analysis under weakly-informative priors confirms the contrasts

To confirm these conclusions are not artefacts of the frequentist framework or of the near-complete separation in the strongest contrast, we refitted the positivity, depth-controlled detection and productivity models as Bayesian logistic regressions under weakly-informative priors (Normal(0, 2.5) on the log-odds coefficients; Methods), summarising each effect by its posterior median odds ratio, 95% credible interval (CrI) and posterior probability of direction (Table S3). The contamination enrichment and the trace excess were reproduced essentially unchanged and with near-certainty (cell-line OR 5.2 [3.6, 7.3], engineered OR 4.6 [2.8, 7.4], neoplasia trace OR 1.9 [1.6, 2.4]; each with P(OR > 1) > 0.999). Crucially, the productive-controls-versus-skin contrast, whose frequentist odds ratio (10,183) is inflated and unstable under separation, regularised to a finite but still enormous posterior OR of 8,785 [2,887, 30,272] (14,515 [3,961, 77,562] under a heavier-tailed Student-t prior): the productive gap between warts/EV and skin is real, not a separation artefact. Deeper sequencing within neoplasia again bought no productive-level detection (OR 1.7 [0.2, 16], P(OR > 1) = 0.685), and the warts/EV-versus-neoplasia productivity contrast held (OR 3.7 [1.3, 11], P(OR > 1) = 0.991). The neoplasia-versus-skin comparison at floor level, whose frequentist interval is wide because it rests on 6 above-floor libraries, shrinks under the prior but stays clearly positive (OR 12 [3.7, 39], P(OR > 1) = >0.999): the small floor-level elevation of neoplasia over clean skin is genuine. It is nonetheless negligible beside the near-four-orders-of-magnitude productive-control effect, and it does not alter the trace-not-productive conclusion.

Discussion

By systematically re-mining public human RNA-seq, recovering the non-human reads that standard transcriptomic pipelines discard, we resolved the productive status of cutaneous HPV across the spectrum from healthy skin to carcinoma, while controlling for the two confounders that have dogged this question: laboratory contamination and sequencing depth. Three findings stand out. First, HPV signal in archived RNA-seq is dominated by cell-line and engineered material and by the integrated mucosal types HPV16/HPV18, so that genuine primary skin carries HPV at only 2–4%. Second, and centrally, HPV in cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC/AK) is present only as a transcriptionally inactive trace, not as productive infection, and this gap is not an artefact of how deeply the libraries were sequenced. Third, the same assay readily detects productive infection where it genuinely occurs: in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), and in a minority of bona fide primary-skin lesions carrying gamma- and alpha-HPV.

Trace, not productive: the transcriptomic phenotype of cutaneous neoplasia

The defining prediction of the “hit-and-run” hypothesis is that beta-HPV acts early in cutaneous carcinogenesis but is dispensable for tumour maintenance, so that viral load and transcription decline as lesions progress and are minimal or absent in established carcinoma (Howley and Pfister 2015). The experimental backbone of this model is genetic: in transgenic and infection systems, deleting the viral oncogenes after lesions have formed, or transplanting secondary tumours, leaves carcinoma growth unaffected and viral genomes undetectable (Viarisio et al. 2018; Dorfer et al. 2021), and in human tissue viral load and transcription are highest in early precursor lesions and fall in established tumours (Borgogna et al. 2018). Our data provide a complementary, population-scale transcriptomic read-out of the same prediction. Across 406 cSCC/AK libraries, only 6 reached the control-calibrated detection floor (1.5%), against 93.2% of productive controls, and the tier’s median burden was 0.012 RPM against 5,408 RPM in controls. Neoplasia does carry HPV more often than clean skin, both as a trace signal (any read; OR 2.0, P = 5.5×10⁻¹⁰) and, marginally, at the detection floor (OR 14, P = 6.7×10⁻⁶; halved to OR 7.5 once the 3 mucosal HPV16 cases are removed). But that elevation is a rise from near-zero to near-zero, and it is not converted into productive burden by any amount of sequencing. This is the residual footprint, rather than active infection, that hit-and-run predicts. It is not, however, evidence for that model over its competitors, for reasons set out below. This is not a new observation, and we do not present it as one. Transcriptional silence of HPV in cutaneous carcinoma has now been reported from four independent RNA-sequencing series: the original cSCC transcriptome study (Arron et al. 2011), total RNA sequencing of skin lesions at a median 66 million reads (Hultin et al. 2019), whole-transcriptome analysis of 345 post-transplant non-melanoma skin cancers at a median 35 million reads with transcription in 15 (Arroyo Mühr, Hultin, and Dillner 2021), and RNA sequencing of 23 risk-stratified cSCC biopsies with no HPV expression against 64% DNA positivity in the same samples (Vandiver et al. 2021), the DNA-present/RNA-absent dissociation we report here with the paired modality our design cannot supply. An orthogonal assay agrees at comparable cohort size: E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization across 243 cutaneous SCC detected high-risk transcripts in 0.9% of the 225 non-anogenital cases (Fujimoto et al. 2019). Two of the sequencing series ran at medians of 35 and 66 million reads, and so had already disposed of the possibility that this negative is an artefact of shallow sequencing. Nor is the literature unanimous: in situ hybridization on PCR-positive transplant-recipient cSCC demonstrated EV-HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 tumours, localised to the mid and upper epidermis (Purdie et al. 2005), a focal, suprabasal signal that bulk sequencing of a whole biopsy averages away and that our design would not recover.

What our data add is not the direction of the result but its denominator, its controls and its criterion. The prior transcriptomic series run from 11 to 345 specimens; ours covers 406 cSCC/AK libraries against 7,800 unselected-skin libraries in the same pipeline, which converts an absence reported within lesions into a case/control contrast with an estimated effect size. The largest prior series is confined to formalin-fixed material from transplant recipients; ours is restricted to neither, so the result is not conditional on immunosuppression or on archival fixation. And where the prior work scores HPV presence or transcription, we score productive replication from late capsid transcripts against a floor calibrated on lesions in which productive infection is certain, so that “no productive infection in cSCC/AK” is measured on the same instrument that reports 93.2% productivity in warts rather than asserted from a null result. The depth argument likewise changes role: it is no longer the discovery that depth was not the explanation, which Arroyo Mühr, Hultin, and Dillner (2021) had already established, but a modelled covariate across that contrast, and the neoplasia libraries were in any case sequenced almost four times more deeply than the productive controls (median 45.2M vs 12.2M reads), with even the deepest, at 327.3M reads, not crossing the productive threshold.

That said, transcriptomic absence cannot by itself adjudicate the mechanism, and the reason is sharper than a general appeal to correlation. The decline of viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma is not the discriminating observation it was once taken to be, because all three live accounts predict it.

Under hit-and-run, activity falls because the virus is dispensable once the tumour is established (Howley and Pfister 2015; Viarisio et al. 2018; Dorfer et al. 2021). Under the protective-immunity account, it falls because virus-positive cells are selected against: the original report already showed reduced beta-HPV activity and load in human skin cancer relative to adjacent healthy skin (Strickley et al. 2019), and the mechanism has since been resolved further, with papillomavirus colonisation blocking the expansion of mutant p53 clones in a CD8+ T-cell-dependent manner, beta-HPV activity elevated in sun-exposed human skin bearing such clones, and clonal expansion in premalignant lesions associated with loss of beta-HPV (Son et al. 2025). A falling viral signal along the progression axis is therefore a shared prediction, and our data, which measure exactly that axis, cannot separate the two. That work also reports beta-HPV activity elevated in sun-exposed human skin, which sits in apparent tension with the quiet reservoir we describe. The two measurements are not commensurate: theirs is in situ viral activity in the epidermis, localised to keratinocyte clones in UV-damaged skin, whereas ours is a whole-biopsy bulk average over archived libraries with no stratification by UV exposure, and a focal signal confined to a small clonal compartment is precisely what such an average dilutes. Our healthy-skin figure should therefore be read as a population-level transcript abundance in unselected skin, not as a claim that no keratinocyte anywhere is transcribing beta-HPV. We note also that the protective-immunity claim is itself contested in the primary literature, having drawn a Matters Arising and a reply in the same journal (Lambert et al. 2021; Strickley et al. 2021), so presenting it as one settled half of a two-way contest would misdescribe the field.

A third account requires no oncogenic or immunological premise at all. The beta-HPV genome restricts its own gene expression and replication through the viral E8^E2 protein, and immortalisation of human keratinocytes by a beta-HPV genome requires that repressor to be inactivated as well as E6, E7, E1 and E2 to be present (Rehm et al. 2022). On that reading, a transcriptionally quiet beta-HPV genome in skin is the virus in its default state, and quiescence carries no information about oncogenic mechanism whatsoever. Our observation that the cutaneous reservoir is episomal and quiet in healthy skin, and remains quiet in neoplasia, is consistent with this without requiring it.

What our data therefore establish is not a verdict between models but the phenomenology all of them must accommodate, measured rather than assumed: established cutaneous neoplasia does not host productive HPV infection. 1.5% of cSCC/AK libraries reach the productive floor, against 93.2% of lesions in which productive infection is certain, and that gap is independent of sequencing depth and of library chemistry. Our cross-sectional snapshot of bulk transcription measures viral activity, not causation, and cannot distinguish a virus that has “hit and run” from one that was selected against by immunity, or from one that was never transcriptionally active to begin with.

One line of evidence does go beyond observation, and it is worth stating precisely what it shows. In a double-blind randomised sham-controlled trial, 70 immunocompetent adults with 15 or more actinic keratoses received a nine-valent papillomavirus vaccine or sham. Lesion-burden reductions were greater in the vaccinated group at 6 and 12 months (47% versus 29%, P = 0.01; 58% versus 47%, P = 0.05), with fewer thick lesions, and no difference in the rate of new lesions or in keratinocyte-carcinoma incidence over the year (Wenande et al. 2025). This is the interventional experiment a cross-sectional transcriptomic survey cannot perform, and it shows that manipulating papillomavirus immunity changes precancerous lesion burden. It is not evidence that beta-HPV is productively replicating in those lesions, and it does not identify the virus responsible: the vaccine targets nine mucosal alphapapillomavirus types, none of them the cutaneous beta-types that dominate the skin reservoir, so any effect must run through cross-reactive or non-specific immunity rather than through neutralising the resident virus. Our result is consistent with that reading rather than in tension with it, since an immunological intervention can reduce lesion burden without productive viral replication being present to target.

Productive cutaneous HPV is real, but it is the property of warts and EV

The trace-level neoplasia result is not a failure of sensitivity. The assay recovered abundant productive infection in the positive-control lesions: 64% of targeted wart/EV libraries met the strict L1 major-capsid criterion, spanning the expected cutaneous repertoire (HPV2/27/57, HPV6/11, and diverse beta/gamma types), consistent with the differentiation-coupled late programme that defines productive papillomavirus infection (Doorbar et al. 2012; Egawa and Doorbar 2017). The contrast between productive controls and neoplasia was significant (OR 3.8, P = 0.013). A small number of genuine, non-cell-line skin lesions also harboured unambiguous productive infection, most strikingly an HPV12-productive cSCC and two lesions co-infected with the gamma types HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. These cases matter for two reasons. They confirm that bona fide productive cutaneous beta/gamma infection occurs in primary tissue and can be detected from public RNA-seq, which answers the original descriptive question about productive infection. The companion question about non-traditional tissues is not answered here: every one of these libraries is cutaneous, and the residual tier that would have to supply non-cutaneous evidence is defined by missing site metadata rather than by an identified site elsewhere, so this design can bound HPV activity in skin but cannot survey the tissues outside it. They also show that the population-level “trace” conclusion is a statement about the central tendency of cSCC/AK, not a claim that productive cutaneous HPV disease never exists. The picture that emerges aligns with the commensal model of cutaneous HPV (Antonsson et al. 2000; Foulongne et al. 2012): a ubiquitous but transcriptionally quiet beta/gamma reservoir in normal skin, overt productive disease confined to warts and EV, and only a residual footprint in carcinoma.

What a 2-4% transcriptome prevalence means against a 90% DNA reservoir

Our primary-skin figure of 2-4% sits against a DNA literature reporting cutaneous beta-HPV in the large majority of healthy adults, and the gap is wide enough that it has to be addressed directly rather than filed under limitations. It is not a contradiction, because the two numbers measure different things, and three published quantities show why.

The first is abundance. Quantitative PCR of eyebrow hair follicles across 782 immunocompetent people and organ-transplant recipients found median beta-HPV DNA loads below one viral copy per 60 cells, spanning seven orders of magnitude (Weissenborn et al. 2012). A commensal carried at that density is below the detection floor of bulk RNA sequencing by construction: even under perfect transcription, one genome per 60 cells contributes a vanishing fraction of a library’s reads. Most of the DNA assays reporting high prevalence are type-specific PCR amplifications designed to find exactly this, and they are orders of magnitude more sensitive than untargeted sequencing of total RNA; the untargeted metagenomic survey that also reports high skin prevalence sampled skin-surface sites (Ma et al. 2014), which brings in the second difference.

The second is substrate. The standard substrates of cutaneous beta-HPV epidemiology are surface skin swabs and plucked eyebrow hair bulbs, and the choice between them changes the answer: in the same 370 individuals, beta-HPV prevalence was 92% in swabs against 73% in eyebrow hairs, and gamma-HPV 84% against 43% (Rollison, Schell, et al. 2019). Both sample the follicular and superficial compartments where the commensal reservoir resides. Our substrate is neither. Archived RNA-seq libraries are made from biopsy or excision tissue, which is dominated by the dermis and the viable epidermis and largely excludes the surface and follicular material that swabs and hair bulbs are designed to capture. Our 2-4% is therefore a statement about papillomavirus transcript abundance within intra-epidermal biopsy tissue, not an estimate of the reservoir as the DNA literature defines and samples it.

The third is the reference panel. Deep sequencing of human skin has catalogued 396 HPV types, of which 229 were previously unknown (Bzhalava et al. 2014), whereas typing here is anchored on the PaVE reference set of 455 sequences. Types with no reference genome cannot be assigned by any panel-based method, so our prevalence is a floor with respect to cutaneous diversity as well as to abundance, and the trace-level detections that resolve to a confident type (Table S6) are the visible edge of a wider reservoir rather than its full extent.

Read together, these place the 2-4% where it belongs: as the transcriptionally detectable fraction of a reservoir that is genuinely near-ubiquitous at DNA level, and not as a competing prevalence estimate. That distinction matters beyond bookkeeping, because it is the same distinction the paper draws for neoplasia. Prospective work makes the point from the DNA side: among 1,008 individuals followed after baseline skin-swab typing, beta-HPV detection predicted subsequent cutaneous SCC, yet fewer than 5% of the beta-HPV types found on a person’s skin were present in the tumour that person later developed (Rollison et al. 2021). A second cohort, in a different population and with paired sampling by site, reaches the same conclusion: across 193 samples from organ-transplant recipients and immunocompetent patients with cSCC, 65 HPV genotypes were recovered, 56 of them from eyebrow hair against 30 from the carcinomas, and genotype-specific concordance between a patient’s eyebrow hair and their own cSCC was found in 5 of 55 patients (9.1%) (Oh et al. 2026). The commensal reservoir is richer than the tumour and largely not the same virus, which is what our transcriptomic data show at population scale and from the activity side.

Actinic keratosis, HPV8, and what a bulk transcriptome cannot see

The precursor end of the neoplasia tier deserves separate treatment, because a specific hit-and-run mechanism has been built on it. In mouse models, the HPV8 E6 protein binds p300 and phosphorylates STAT3, inducing ΔNp63 and driving proliferation and expansion of Lrig1+ hair-follicle junctional-zone keratinocyte stem cells into the overlying epidermis; HPV8 was reported in association with 70% of human actinic keratoses, and the authors frame the expansion of these melanosome-poor, UV-vulnerable stem cells as the hit-and-run mechanism itself (Morgan et al. 2024).

On presence, we do not disagree. Trace HPV reads were recovered from 62.5% of our 72 AK libraries, which is the same order as their 70% association figure. Our result concerns what that material is doing, and the answer is the same in AK as in carcinoma: 1 of 72 AK libraries reached the productive floor.

That is not a contradiction of their model, and is closer to a corroboration of it. A mechanism driven by E6 acting on a stem-cell compartment requires viral oncogene function, not capsid production, and a hit-and-run account predicts precisely that the virus leaves no productive footprint in the lesion it helped initiate. Our data supply the population-scale version of that prediction and find it satisfied.

Two things we cannot settle are worth stating plainly. The first is type. We detected no HPV8 anywhere in the cohort: no library met the assignment criterion for it, and it was the best-hit reference in none of the 325 trace-level libraries, although HPV8 is present in the reference panel and other beta-1 types including HPV5 and HPV12 were recovered. Whether that reflects genuine absence of HPV8 transcription, cohort composition, or the fact that DNA association and transcript detection need not coincide, we cannot determine from RNA alone. The second is compartment.
