The Lrig1+ junctional zone is a follicular structure, and it is exactly the compartment that our substrate under-samples: it is what plucked eyebrow-hair-bulb assays are designed to capture and what an excision biopsy dominated by dermis and interfollicular epidermis dilutes. A focal, follicular, stem-cell-restricted reservoir is the case our design is least able to see, and the negative we report for AK should be read with that limit attached.

Contamination is the dominant signal in naïve analyses

Our cell-line finding is both a result and a methodological warning. The roughly five-fold enrichment of HPV positivity in cell-line and engineered libraries, dominated by HPV16/HPV18, mirrors the documented contamination of public sequence archives by HeLa-derived and other integrated-HPV reads (Adey et al. 2013; Cantalupo, Katz, and Pipas 2015; Kazemian et al. 2015). Where that contamination has been traced to its source, the mechanism is exactly the one our enrichment implies: applying a virus-detection workflow to 9,143 TCGA RNA-seq libraries from a single sequencing centre attributed the HeLa-derived HPV18 signal, and a co-occurring XMRV signal, to a pool of cell lines run alongside the tumours as a quality-control reference, so that the tumours carrying those reads were not infected at all (Selitsky et al. 2020). Our result is the same phenomenon at the scale of the whole archive rather than one centre, and without the laboratory metadata that allowed that study to name the culprit. Nor is the problem confined to cell lines: systematically sequencing the laboratory components themselves showed that more than 65% of viral sequences recovered from 712 libraries fell into clusters linked to a reagent or protocol step rather than to the specimen (Asplund et al. 2019), which is why a detection floor calibrated on genuine productive lesions, rather than on the absence of reads, is doing necessary work here. Any survey that pools archived data without flagging non-primary material and without coverage-breadth and depth thresholds will substantially overstate HPV prevalence and mis-attribute mucosal high-risk types to tissues where they have no biological place. The cost of getting this wrong at archive scale is not hypothetical: re-analysis of the reported pan-cancer microbiome found that most of the microbes originally called were not present in the samples at all, invalidating the original report and more than a dozen studies built on it (Gihawi et al. 2023). None of the individual safeguards we applied is novel, and the requirements have been set out before in reviews of virus detection in sequence data (Cantalupo and Pipas 2019). What we contribute is their operationalisation and measurement on one cohort: explicit cell-line, engineered and in-vitro annotation, study-level curation, dual breadth-and-depth typing thresholds, a control-calibrated productivity floor, and burden normalised for both depth and library chemistry, with the size of the artefact each is guarding against reported rather than asserted. That combination generalises beyond HPV.

What the integration marker measures

Reading integration from the relative abundance of viral genes is not new, and the marker used here should be located against that work rather than presented as an invention. In cervical disease, the ratio of E2 to E6 is an established surrogate for physical integration status: measured on cytology specimens from 226 HPV16-positive women it falls with lesion grade, from 0.79 in both normal epithelium and CIN1 to 0.48 in CIN2/3 and 0.36 in carcinoma, discriminating CIN2 or worse with an area under the curve of 0.844, and it declines alongside L1 capsid immunoreactivity (Choi et al. 2018). The underlying biology, that the integrated fraction rises with lesion severity, is older still (Cheung et al. 2008). The step from DNA ratios to transcript ratios has also been taken: integration status in head and neck squamous carcinoma has been classified from spliced virus-host fusion transcripts and from ratios of HPV gene transcripts across 261 RNA-seq samples in five cohorts, with DNA integration events in 102 participants as ground truth (Li et al. 2026). The more general move, grading integration by its transcriptional output rather than its presence, is also established: in cervical cancer, integration sites that generate fusion transcripts behave differently from silent ones, and the productive fraction rises from carcinoma in situ to advanced disease (Fan et al. 2023). Our cervical validation series reproduces that direction from a different measurement, which is a point in its favour rather than a novelty claim. What is specific to this study is narrower than the concept: an E1 numerator against an E2 denominator taken from bulk RNA-seq read counts, applied to cutaneous beta- and gamma-types in skin, and used as a provenance check rather than a clinical classifier. Even so, a marker that only ever fired on cultured cells would be indistinguishable from the metadata-based flagging it was meant to check independently. The graded cervical series settles that question in the direction that matters. Across HPV16-positive normal epithelium, high-grade lesion and carcinoma, sequenced under one protocol and labelled by the submitting study, the ratio moves monotonically with grade in primary tissue with no cell line anywhere in the series, and late transcription falls away along the same axis. The marker is therefore reading integration as a biological process rather than culture as a provenance, which is what licenses its use on skin: when it reports the cutaneous reservoir as episomal and quiet, that is a statement about the virus, not an echo of how the libraries were annotated. The series is small, and the normal-epithelium arm in particular rests on few informative libraries, so it establishes the direction of the marker rather than a calibrated scale. A second and more consequential limit comes from the cervical literature that established the ratio in the first place. An E2 deficit is not specific to advanced disease: triplex quantitative PCR for E6, E2 and beta-globin indicated integration in 44.3% of histologically negative control samples in a series of 380 women, with substantial overlap between cases and controls that precluded any usable cutoff (Boulet et al. 2009), and serial sampling of women recruited soon after first intercourse showed E2 disruption to be a common and early event in incident infection, occurring within months and more often for HPV18 than HPV16 (Collins et al. 2009). Our inferential chain runs from a high E1:E2 to an episomal reservoir, and that chain is only as strong as the specificity of the deficit it inverts. One difference works in our favour without settling the matter: those studies measure DNA copy-number ratios, in which a minor integrated subclone can depress the ratio while the bulk population remains episomal, whereas we measure transcript ratios, which report what the viral population is actually expressing. Whether that makes the transcript form less susceptible to the early-integration confound is a reasonable expectation rather than something demonstrated here, and until it is tested the marker should be read as evidence about the dominant transcriptional state of the reservoir, not as a proof that no integrated genome is present. It is also worth being explicit about what the cervical data are not doing here. They are not a matched mucosal counterpart to the skin cohort, and the two are not contrasted quantitatively: the comparison that carries weight is within the cervical progression itself, where the confounders that separate any two archived cohorts, depth, protocol, selection and provenance, are held constant by design.

What a petabase catalogue does and does not measure

The DNA axis used here is a catalogue, and catalogues answer a narrower question than they appear to. The Logan-wide papillomavirus survey identifies contigs by profile-HMM filtering with identification of the conserved L1 B and I domains (J. Y. Q. Shen et al. 2026), over an assembly of 27 million archived sequencing libraries (Chikhi et al. 2024), so a contig enters the catalogue because it carries a detectable L1. Three consequences follow, and together they bound what any comparison against such a resource can claim. First, presence in the catalogue means L1-detectable presence, and carries no information about the state of the viral genome. Second, the catalogue is assembly-based, and an integrated genome cannot assemble across the virus-host junction, so integrated molecules are systematically under-recovered: conditioning on near-complete contigs returns an intact E2 in 99.3% of cervical carcinoma contigs against 99.9% in skin (Table S8), which is close to a tautology rather than a biological result, because the completeness criterion has already selected episomal genomes in both. Third, because every contig is anchored on L1 and extends outward from it, the frequency with which an open reading frame is truncated at a contig terminus tracks its distance from that anchor rather than the position of any breakpoint; the ordering E1 > E2 > L1 holds in every body site examined, including healthy vaginal and gut carriage, where integration cannot explain it. Genome state therefore has to be read from reads or from transcription rather than from catalogue membership, which is what the E1:E2 ratio and the virus-host junctions do above. The point generalises beyond papillomaviruses: petabase-scale surveys are now the standard way to establish that a virus is present in a body site, and a presence count from such a survey is not evidence of an active infection.

Strengths and limitations

The principal strengths of this work are its scale, its uniform end-to-end processing of heterogeneous public data, and its explicit control of the depth, chemistry and contamination confounders that limit prior reports. Recovering discarded non-human reads turns a vast existing resource toward a question it was never collected to answer (Edgar et al. 2022), and reading productivity directly from the early/late transcript programme provides a biologically grounded activity measure rather than mere presence/absence. That last point is where this work sits relative to the two prior archive-scale mining studies of skin. Screening off-target reads across 19 skin tumour types was a search for a driver, and found one, in an acral tumour outside the beta-HPV question entirely (Leiendecker et al. 2023); reprocessing 8,274 public skin libraries catalogued HPV among the foreign RNA of skin without typing it, scoring its productivity or setting it against a case/control design (Bhargava et al. 2025). Both establish that the substrate is rich. Neither asks, and neither can answer, at what rate cutaneous HPV is transcribed across the spectrum from healthy skin to carcinoma and whether that transcription is productive, which is the question this study is built around.

Several limitations temper interpretation. First, the unbiased prevalence sweep screened 11,556 libraries, a large but not exhaustive sample of public human skin RNA-seq: of roughly 12,200 candidate runs discovered, the remainder were lost to withdrawn accessions, download failures or quality-control exclusion, and archival sampling is itself non-random, so the absolute healthy-skin positivity rate is best read as an estimate. Second, library-selection chemistry biases viral recovery, and although we measured it rather than assuming it away, we could not measure it everywhere. Chemistry was resolvable for 62.2% of libraries; for the remainder the SRA record and the submitted protocol text are both silent, and those libraries carry the trace signal alongside the resolved ones. Where it is known, the axis of concern is flat: rRNA-depleted libraries were no more likely than poly-A libraries to carry an HPV read at equal depth (OR 1.0, 0.8–1.2), and the tier reported here as non-productive is the one more often built with the favourable chemistry. What this does not settle is the rest of library construction. Selection chemistry is only one axis: input amount, RNA integrity and fragment-size selection are not recoverable from archived metadata at all, and a poly-A-selected library remains, in principle, a conservative instrument for late viral transcripts. Absence of HPV reads is therefore not proof of absence of virus, and our productivity estimates remain conservative. Third, bulk sequencing of a whole biopsy averages over every cell in it, so transcription confined to a small, focal cell fraction is diluted below detection. This is not hypothetical for cutaneous HPV: in situ hybridization localises EV-HPV transcripts to the mid and upper epidermal layers of cSCC (Purdie et al. 2005), precisely the spatially restricted, suprabasal pattern that a whole-biopsy average is least able to see. Our productivity estimates are therefore a lower bound on focal transcription, and the negative we report is a statement about population-level viral burden rather than about every cell in every tumour. Fourth, tissue and diagnosis labels were derived programmatically from sample metadata and are imperfect, despite curation; residual misclassification adds noise to the tier assignments. Fifth, typing is anchored on a fixed reference panel, and deep sequencing of skin has described 229 HPV types that had no reference genome at the time of that survey (Bzhalava et al. 2014); such types are invisible to any panel-based assignment, so our type catalogue and prevalence are bounded by the panel as well as by detection sensitivity. Sixth, the high sequence similarity among HPV types permits cross-mapping, which we mitigated with breadth/depth thresholds and multimapping-aware alignment but cannot wholly exclude; the same caveat attaches to distinguishing low-level true infection from residual contaminant signal at the detection floor. Seventh, our data are transcriptomic and cross-sectional: we cannot observe viral DNA persistence, integration state, or the temporal decline in viral activity that the hit-and-run model specifies, and we therefore describe the productive-status phenomenology rather than prove the mechanism. Finally, the L1-based productivity rule, while deliberately stringent, depends on beta/gamma gene annotation quality and treats integrated-line L1 signal cautiously (reported only in the supplement).

Conclusion

Mining the reads that transcriptomic studies routinely throw away, we find that the cutaneous HPV reservoir of healthy skin is real but transcriptionally quiet, that productive cutaneous HPV infection is the property of warts and EV, and that HPV in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, at population scale and independent of both sequencing depth and library chemistry, is a trace, non-productive footprint rather than an active infection. This transcriptomic phenotype is the common ground that every current account of beta-HPV in skin cancer must explain, whether the virus is a departed cofactor, the target of protective immunity, or a genome that is transcriptionally restricted by default. Because a declining viral signal is predicted by all three, separating them will not be achieved by measuring viral activity more precisely. It will require designs that break the shared prediction: matched DNA- and RNA-level profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, resolution of where the residual virus resides relative to mutant clones and to infiltrating T cells, linkage to host antiviral immunity in the same tissue, and interventional studies of the kind the VAXAK trial has now begun (Wenande et al. 2025). The single-cell assay is not itself the missing piece: HPV transcripts have already been resolved to basal keratinocytes, suprabasal keratinocytes and hair-follicle stem cells within a cutaneous lesion by single-cell RNA sequencing (Devitt et al. 2019). What has not been done is to apply it at cohort scale across the actinic-keratosis-to-carcinoma transition in beta- and gamma-positive lesions, which is where a shared prediction of declining activity would finally come apart into distinguishable ones. The public-archive mining framework developed here, with its contamination controls and its normalisation for both depth and library chemistry, provides a scalable foundation for identifying the cohorts worth taking to that resolution.

Supplementary Material

Above-floor HPV in tissue that cannot host it: two contaminated studies

The non-permissive tissue tier is defined by biology, not by its HPV content, so it also exposes the opposite case: libraries from non-permissive material that carry HPV above the trace level. Two studies do, and both were held out of the control tier for that reason.

SRP572742 (skeletal muscle and blood from myotonic dystrophy patients, n = 66) is HPV-positive at any level in 83% of libraries, with 3 crossing the control-calibrated detection floor and a maximum of 5.3 RPM. Neither muscle nor blood contains stratified squamous epithelium, so no part of that signal can be infection of the sampled tissue.

SRP565659 makes the point under internal control. It is a multi-omic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma study in which skin and peripheral blood were taken from the same patients and sequenced together (Table S1 of the source publication assigns every run a tissue). Its 26 skin libraries are strongly HPV-positive, 88% at any level and up to 12.0 RPM, as expected for lesional skin. Its 42 blood and lymph-node libraries (same patients, same runs, tissue that cannot host the virus) are HPV-positive at 52%, up to 3.6 RPM, with one library above the floor.

The pattern in both is a minority of reads appearing in libraries with no biological source for them, alongside co-sequenced libraries carrying a genuine high-titre signal. That is the signature of index hopping and inter-library carry-over rather than infection, and it is the same phenomenon that makes cell-line contamination the dominant driver of apparent HPV positivity in public transcriptomes. Two consequences follow for how the trace signal should be read. First, a non-zero HPV read count in a single library is not evidence of infection even when the tissue is plausible, which is why the analysis here is anchored on a control-calibrated floor rather than on detection. Second, studies whose design places high-titre and HPV-free material in the same sequencing run will inflate apparent prevalence in the HPV-free arm, so prevalence estimates drawn from public data without a non-permissive control are upper bounds.
